title: How HTTPS keeps a secret in public

scenes.say: Every time you see the little lock in your browser, two computers that had never met just agreed on a secret, while anyone on the network could be listening. How is that even possible?

visual.title: How HTTPS keeps a secret in public
visual.subtitle: The lock icon, in plain words

scenes.heading: The problem
scenes.say: Plain HTTP is like a postcard. Every network along the way can read it, and can even change it. HTTPS is a sealed envelope. Only the two ends can read it, and any tampering is detected.

items.text: A postcard: anyone on the route can read it
A sealed envelope: only the two ends read it

scenes.heading: The trick
scenes.say: Here is the trick, explained with paint. Mixing two paints is easy, but un-mixing them is practically impossible. That one-way step is the whole secret.

right.label: Mixing paint
right.sub: easy to mix, impossible to un-mix

scenes.say: Both sides start from the same public color. Each one secretly mixes in a private color, and sends the mixture across. Then each adds its own secret color once more. Both land on exactly the same final color, but anyone watching only ever saw the mixtures. In real HTTPS the colors are huge numbers, and un-mixing them would take today's computers longer than the age of the universe.

visual.caption: Each side keeps its secret color. Only mixtures travel.

scenes.heading: The handshake
scenes.say: So the handshake goes like this. Your browser says hello and sends its paint mixture. The server replies with its own mixture, plus a certificate that proves who it is, like an ID card. Both now hold the same secret key, and everything after that is encrypted.
All of this happens on port four forty-three, the door your browser knocks on for HTTPS. Plain HTTP uses port eighty.

scenes.heading: Faster too
scenes.say: Newer versions are faster, too. TLS one point two needs two round trips before your data can flow. TLS one point three needs just one. And a resumed connection can send data right away.

scenes.heading: A short history
scenes.say: The lock has been evolving for about thirty years. SSL arrived in nineteen ninety-five. TLS replaced it in ninety-nine. Version one point two came in two thousand eight, and one point three in twenty eighteen.

scenes.heading: What snoopers see
scenes.say: And this is what someone snooping on the network actually sees. A tiny header that says, encrypted data follows, and then bytes that look like pure noise.

scenes.heading: The catch
scenes.say: So the lock is a promise about the connection. But here is the catch.
The lock means the line is private. It does not mean the site is honest. A scam site can have a perfectly valid certificate too.

visual.text: The lock means the line is private. Not that the site is honest.

scenes.heading: Recap
scenes.say: So, three things to remember. The secret key is never sent, it is mixed. The certificate proves who you are talking to. And the lock protects the line, not the truth.

items.text: The key is mixed, never sent
The certificate proves who is talking
The lock protects the line, not the truth
